nodes.label: SponsorX Plain English Explainer
nodes.author: BTG Sports Group
nodes.rationale: Positioning and messaging reference, September 2026, internal. Ten-second version: local athletes already have your customers' attention; SponsorX rents you that attention as a package, at a fixed price, with proof it worked.

nodes.label: Bundled Athlete Network Model
nodes.rationale: The two-sided problem: one athlete with 20,000 followers is not worth the hassle of a contract, but ten of them is a real campaign — with ten contracts, ten negotiations and ten people to chase; meanwhile the athlete has a real engaged audience but is too small for a brand to bother with. SponsorX sits in the middle and bundles them: many small audiences become one sellable thing, and one business deals with one invoice. The business never finds an athlete, negotiates a rate, writes a contract, or chases a deliverable.

nodes.label: Five-Step Campaign Flow
nodes.rationale: 1) Business states goal and budget. 2) SponsorX picks athletes from the roster — matched to neighbourhood and customers, not by follower count but by who actually gets engagement and reliably delivers. 3) Athletes make content; the sponsor approves everything before it goes public. 4) Fans get an offer: each athlete gets their own code; a fan scans, claims, and redeems in-store. 5) The business gets the numbers — views, engagement, scans, claims, redemptions — per athlete, so they know who moved the needle.

nodes.label: Redemption as Proof (The Differentiator)
nodes.rationale: Step four is the one thing that makes it different: every other form of local sponsorship ends at 'your logo was seen'; this one ends at '1,870 people used your code'. That is the whole pitch — everything else is a feature; this is the reason to believe. Answer to 'how do I know it worked?': because the offer is redeemed in your store. Not impressions. Redemptions.

nodes.label: Athlete Value Proposition
nodes.rationale: Paid for content you are half-making already; you pick each job — nothing is automatic and you can say no with no penalty; not exclusive — your own deals stay yours, this is not signing your career over to an agency; under 18 requires a parent or guardian to approve before anything happens; you can see what you have earned and exactly where it stands.

nodes.label: Sponsor Objection Handling
nodes.rationale: Four expected objections: price — start at $750, three athletes, one post each, a real report, deliberately cheap enough to say yes without a meeting; 'just influencer marketing?' — no, influencers rent an audience, athletes rent standing in a community (a kid people watch play on Friday night carries weight a random creator does not); proof — in-store redemption, not impressions; brand risk — the sponsor approves every piece before publication.

nodes.label: Do Not Lead With Reach
nodes.rationale: The current homepage says '1.2M Monthly Reach / 2.4M Fans Engaged' — the old pitch, selling audience size, which invites comparison to buying ads, a game you lose on price. The current strategy sells outcomes: lead with '$750, three athletes, and a number you can check'.

nodes.label: Pilot Campaigns as Proof-Building
nodes.rationale: Four anchor athletes, no completed campaigns yet. The first five campaigns are not sales, they are proof-building — price them as pilots and get written permission to publish the numbers. Until then, do not imply results you do not have; the case-study slots on the homepage are deliberately empty for exactly this reason. Figures used in the explainer are illustrative, not results.
